overview.intro:
Chapter 14 covers raw plant materials that are not food: **bamboo, rattan, willow (osier), raffia, reeds and cereal straw** used for weaving and basketry (heading 1401), and a catch-all heading 1404 for **cotton linters, vegetable hair, broomcorn, istle** and other broom fibres, and "vegetable products not elsewhere specified" — which CBP rulings place coco peat and coir pith, dried henna leaves and dried hemp flower in. Its **14 tariff lines** are mostly Free; the highest base rate is 4.4% on willow.

The extra duty by country decides the cost. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%** — but every 1404.90.90 line (coco peat, henna, hemp and the rest of the catch-all) is exempt, and several countries have their own exception lists for bamboo, rattan and broom fibres. China adds its 2018–2019 Section 301 duties (**37.5%** in total on bamboo), Brazil 25% more, and **Canada a 50% Section 338 duty** on six Chapter 14 subheadings that applies even to USMCA goods. Mexico, the largest supplier (49% of the $222M imported in 2025), pays nothing on USMCA-qualifying goods.

workedExamples.title: A container of coco peat blocks from Sri Lanka
workedExamples.body: CBP classifies coco peat (coir pith) in 1404.90.90 (rulings N241191, N250256), Free at the general rate. All of 1404.90.90 is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86), so Sri Lanka's 10% rate (9903.05.72) does not apply: a $20,000 container pays **$0** duty. The bags or blocks must still be marked with the country of origin.

workedExamples.title: Bamboo garden stakes: China vs Indonesia
workedExamples.body: Bamboo is Free at the general rate. From China, two Section 301 duties stack: 25% under List 3 (9903.88.03; CBP ruling N318904 applied it to bamboo stakes) and 12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31) — **$3,750** on a $10,000 shipment. The same stakes from Indonesia pay **$0**: 1401.10.00 is on Indonesia's exception list (U.S. note 52(j)(11), 9903.06.16). Bamboo poles must also clear APHIS as a regulated wood article.

workedExamples.title: Coir potting mix from Canada, with a USMCA claim
workedExamples.body: CBP classified a Canadian coco-chip potting mix in 1404.90.90 (N330582). USMCA removes the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93), but 1404.90.90 is on the Canada Section 338 list (U.S. note 51(b)(3), 9903.03.14), and that 50% applies even when USMCA is claimed. A $5,000 shipment entered since August 22, 2026 pays **$2,500**.

workedExamples.title: 20 tonnes of broomcorn from Mexico
workedExamples.body: Broomcorn is $4.95 per tonne — **$99** on 20 t at the general rate, and **$0** with a USMCA claim (plant material grown in Mexico is originating). Without a valid claim, Mexico's 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.55) is added: $99 + $2,400 on a $24,000 load. Broomcorn needs an APHIS import permit, must arrive baled, and may be treated on arrival (7 CFR 319.41).

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover vegetable materials or fibers of vegetable materials of a kind used primarily in the manufacture of textiles, however prepared, or other vegetable materials treated so as to be suitable only as textile materials — those are classified in section XI (for example coir fibre, heading 5305, and true hemp fibre, heading 5302).

**Note 2.** Heading 1401 applies, inter alia, to bamboos (whether or not split, sawn lengthwise, cut to length, rounded at the ends, bleached, rendered nonflammable, polished or dyed), split osier, reeds and the like, to rattan cores and to drawn or split rattans. The heading does not apply to chipwood (heading 4404).

**Note 3.** Heading 1404 does not apply to wood wool (heading 4405) and prepared knots or tufts for broom or brush making (heading 9603).

**Statistical note (1404.90.90.90).** Imports of cigarette wrappers or tubes composed primarily of non-pulped vegetable materials under this provision may be subject to Federal Excise Tax (26 U.S.C. 5701).

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 14 Chapter 14 lines carry the same base rates in both.

What changed came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**, from which all of 1404.90.90 and several countries' bamboo, rattan and broom-fibre lines are exempt. China keeps its 2018–2019 Section 301 duties, Brazil pays another 25%, and since **August 22, 2026 Canada pays 50%** under Section 338 on six subheadings, USMCA claim or not. A new statutory definition of hemp, delayed to **December 11, 2026**, will decide whether dried hemp flower entered under 1404.90.90 can be imported at all.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 14 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their exemption lists, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, China Section 301 Lists 3 and 4A, the Canada Section 338 duty, the Nicaragua Section 301 phase-in, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended; plus agency changes that decide whether goods can enter (Lacey Act declarations, the hemp definition). No antidumping or countervailing duty order and no Section 232 action covers a Chapter 14 line. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 14 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 14 Chapter 14 lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, split or renumbered.

changes.title: China Section 301 Lists 3 and 4A continue
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China Section 301 actions, so they stay in effect during the four-year review. For Chapter 14 this keeps +25% (9903.88.03) on bamboo, willow, other plaiting materials, cotton linters, vegetable hair, istle, other broom fibres and 1404.90.90, and +7.5% (9903.88.15) on rough rattan and broomcorn.

changes.detail: Proclamations 11061–11063 banned some Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy-scope products and motorcycles over 800 cc from September 29, 2026. No Chapter 14 line is on their annexes, so the six subheadings on the Section 338 list keep paying the 50% duty.

changes.title: Section 338 list revised; Chapter 14 lines stay on it
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 added and deleted products on the 9903.03.14 list from September 15, 2026 and made the duty apply on top of Section 232 duties. None of the six Chapter 14 subheadings was removed.

changes.title: New hemp definition delayed to December 11, 2026
changes.detail: Section 781 of P.L. 119-37 redefines hemp (7 U.S.C. 1639o) by total THC, including THCA, of not more than 0.3% on a dry-weight basis, and excludes intermediate products above that level, final products with more than 0.4 mg of THC per container, and synthesized cannabinoids. P.L. 119-103 (September 2, 2026) delayed it to December 11, 2026, except for products with cannabinoids not naturally produced by the plant, which lose hemp status on November 12, 2026. Dried hemp flower and biomass imported under 1404.90.90 that exceed the new limit stop being hemp and become marijuana under the Controlled Substances Act. The tariff rate does not change.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duty of 50% on six Chapter 14 subheadings
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 put a 50% duty (9903.03.14) on Canadian goods in the provisions of U.S. note 51(b)(3), which include bamboo (1401.10.00), willow (1401.90.20), other plaiting materials (1401.90.40), cotton linters (1404.20.00), other broom and brush fibres (1404.90.40) and the whole of 1404.90.90. It is charged even when USMCA is claimed and on top of the 10% Section 301 duty on non-USMCA goods. Planned for August 19, it took effect August 22 after a 3-day suspension (Proclamation 11056).

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover 11 of 14 Chapter 14 lines
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). The three 1404.90.90 lines are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). Country lists in note 52(j) exempt bamboo, rattan or broom fibres of Malaysia, Cambodia, Guatemala, El Salvador, Argentina, Bangladesh, Taiwan, Indonesia, Ecuador, Jordan and Switzerland. EU goods pay 10% in total; USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). FTA claims remove the base rate but not this duty.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired

changes.title: CBP: dried hemp flower is classified in 1404.90.90
changes.detail: In HQ H334131 CBP held that dried, de-stemmed and ground hemp flowers imported for CBD extraction are not a textile material and fall in 1404.90.90 (Free), following earlier rulings that put hemp biomass, hemp leaves and hemp wraps in heading 1404.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), every Chapter 14 line included. The only Chapter 14 exemption is by description: date palm branches, myrtus branches or other vegetable material for religious purposes only (1404.90.90, U.S. note 50(a)(iii), 9903.05.04). From July 24 the 12.5% 2026 action (9903.05.27) is added on top for the other lines.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 14 subheading was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03); only date palm and myrtus branches for religious purposes (1404.90.90) were exempt by description (9903.03.04). changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 14 goods rose from **$201M in 2024 to $222M in 2025** (+10.4%), back above the 2021 peak of $223M after a dip to $162M in 2023. Almost all of it — **$203M, 91%** — is the catch-all 1404.90, which holds broom and brush fibres, vegetable hair and the Free basket line 1404.90.90 that CBP rulings use for coco peat and coir pith, coconut husk chips, dried henna leaves and hemp flower and biomass. The 6-digit trade data does not split it further.

**Mexico supplied $108M (49%)**, all in heading 1404, up 4% and more than double its 2020–2023 level. India ($31M, +52%) and Sri Lanka ($9M, +52%) grew fastest among the large suppliers. Plaiting materials are small and shrinking: bamboo fell 22% to $13M, mostly from China, and rattan to $1.9M; Argentina's 1401 shipments fell 43%. Cotton linters jumped from $0.8M to $3.5M.

Through 2025 USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada paid no extra duty, while most other suppliers paid the IEEPA reciprocal tariff from April 2025. Those duties ended on February 24, 2026; since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5% applies instead, with all of 1404.90.90 exempt. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on Chapter 14 goods depends far more on **where they come from** than on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — computed from the current tariff schedule with the same engine as the tariff calculator.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** (from July 24, 2026). **All of 1404.90.90 is exempt** from it, **USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico enter free**, EU goods pay 10% in total, and **China pays up to 37.5% more**. **Canada is the exception**: a 50% Section 338 duty on bamboo, willow, cotton linters, broom fibres and 1404.90.90 applies even to USMCA goods.

Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

tariffEngineering.h1: Importing Bamboo, Rattan, Cotton Linters, Coco Peat & Hemp (HTS Ch. 14): Rules, Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Bamboo, Rattan, Broomcorn, Coco Peat & Hemp: APHIS, Lacey Act & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 14) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The USDA, CBP, DEA and TTB rules for each HTS Chapter 14 line — APHIS permits for broomcorn and cotton linters, bamboo and rice-straw rules, Lacey Act declarations, the hemp THC limit, excise tax on leaf wraps — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, exception lists, FTAs and AGOA, drawback, rulings.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 14 goods are raw plant material, so **USDA decides whether a shipment clears**: broomcorn and cotton linters need APHIS permits and may be fumigated or treated, bamboo poles are regulated wood articles, rice straw is prohibited without a permit, and bamboo, rattan, willow, broom fibres and tanning materials need a **Lacey Act plant declaration**. Hemp flower must stay under the federal THC limit, which tightens on December 11, 2026.

The ways to pay less are in the schedule: claim **USMCA** on Mexican and Canadian plant material (it does not lift Canada's 50% Section 338 duty), check whether the **country's exception list** covers the line, claim **CAFTA-DR, other FTAs or AGOA** where the base rate is the cost, get a **binding ruling** where the line decides the rate, and claim **drawback** on re-exports. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on plant material from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty for Mexico or Canada plus the base rate (up to 4.4%)
levers.appliesTo: All 14 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in any format. Plants grown and harvested in Mexico or Canada are wholly obtained; processed goods qualify if they change from any other chapter into headings 1401–1404 (General Note 11).
levers.caveat: For Canada, USMCA does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on 1401.10, 1401.90, 1404.20, 1404.90.40 and 1404.90.90 (U.S. note 51(a)). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Source from a country whose exception list covers the line
levers.appliesTo: 1404.90.90 from any of the 60 economies (note 52(b)); bamboo, rattan and broom fibres from the countries named in note 52(j) — e.g. Indonesian, Cambodian or Ecuadorian bamboo and rattan, Swiss or Guatemalan broom fibres
levers.document: Proof of origin for the country claimed (commercial invoice, certificate of origin, production records) and the exemption heading (9903.05.86 or the country heading such as 9903.06.16) on the entry line.
levers.caveat: Origin follows where the goods were grown or substantially transformed; transshipment does not change it. China is on no exception list and keeps its 2018–2019 Section 301 duties.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(b), (j)

levers.title: Claim the FTA or AGOA rate where the base rate is the cost
levers.saves: The base rate: 4.4% (willow), 3.2% (other plaiting materials), 2.3% (broom fibres), 2% (split rattan), 0.5¢/kg or $4.95/t
levers.appliesTo: The six dutiable lines, for goods of CAFTA-DR, Australia, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Panama, Korea, Israel, Jordan, Morocco, Bahrain, Oman, Singapore, CBERA countries and AGOA countries (through December 31, 2026)
levers.document: Proof of origin under the agreement and the SPI on the entry line (P, AU, CL, CO, …, E for CBERA, D for AGOA).
levers.caveat: FTA claims do not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)). GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020, so a GSP claim pays the general rate.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate: raw plaiting material (1401) vs. basketwork (4602), coir pith (1404.90.90, Free, Section 301-exempt) vs. coir fibre (5305), hemp flower (1404.90.90) vs. true hemp fibre (5302)
levers.appliesTo: Any line where classification is in doubt — especially the 1404.90.90 basket provision
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its processing and its use (19 CFR part 177). Published rulings such as N241191 (coco peat), N262445 (henna leaves), N318904 (bamboo stakes) and H334131 (hemp flower) show how CBP decides.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own.

levers.title: Claim drawback when the goods, or what they are made into, are exported
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, including Section 301 duties, on imported materials re-exported or used in exported goods
levers.appliesTo: All lines, when the imported goods or substitutes are exported or used in manufacturing exported goods
levers.document: A drawback claim filed in ACE within 5 years of import, with records linking the import to the export.
levers.caveat: Only duties actually paid are refunded; manufacturing drawback needs a ruling or a general manufacturing ruling.

rules.title: Lacey Act plant declaration (genus, species, country of harvest, quantity, value) for heading 1401, 1404.90.30, 1404.90.40 and 1404.90.90.20/.40 — Phase VII, from December 1, 2024
Bamboo poles and garden stakes are regulated wood articles; sawn or split, dried bamboo free of leaves and seeds enters under a general permit subject to inspection
Broomcorn and other corn and sorghum plant parts: import permit, baled to prevent scattering, inspection and treatment as the inspector requires (European corn borer quarantine)
Cotton linters: entry under the foreign cotton quarantine — vacuum fumigation or movement to an approved mill unless processed (bleached, dyed) so no seed or insect life remains
Rice straw and rice hulls are prohibited from all foreign locations unless APHIS authorizes them under a controlled import permit
Hemp flower and biomass must meet the federal hemp definition (not more than 0.3% delta-9 THC today; total THC incl. THCA from December 11, 2026) or they are marijuana, a controlled substance
Cigarette wrappers or tubes of non-pulped vegetable material (1404.90.90.90) may owe federal excise tax: $0.0315 per 50 papers, $0.0630 per 50 tubes (not in the duty grid)
Henna sold as a color additive is approved only for coloring hair, not skin
Country-of-origin marking on the article or its container (bamboo poles are on the J-list, but their outermost container must be marked)
Wood pallets and crates must be ISPM 15 treated and marked

groups.label: Plaiting materials: bamboo, rattan, willow, raffia, straw
groups.note: Bamboo, rattan, willow and other plaiting materials all need a Lacey Act declaration. Bamboo poles and stakes clear APHIS as regulated wood articles; rice straw needs a controlled import permit.

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 14 FAQ: Bamboo, Rattan, Coco Peat, Cotton Linters & Hemp Import Duties

seo.title: HTS Chapter 14 FAQ 2026: HS Codes for Bamboo, Rattan, Coco Peat, Cotton Linters, Henna & Hemp Flower | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about Chapter 14 imports: HS codes 1401 and 1404.90, bamboo, rattan, coco peat and coir pith, cotton linters, henna, raffia and hemp flower, and the 2026 tariffs from China, Mexico, India and Canada.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing bamboo, rattan, coco peat, cotton linters, broom fibres, henna and hemp into the U.S. — HS codes, tariffs by country and entry rules. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Chapter 14 base rates are low — Free on 8 of 14 lines, 4.4% at most — and unchanged since January 2025. The extra duty by country decides the cost.

Since July 24, 2026 most suppliers pay a 10% or 12.5% Section 301 tariff, but all of 1404.90.90 (coco peat, henna, hemp, other vegetable products) is exempt, and Indonesia, Cambodia, Ecuador and others have exception lists for bamboo, rattan and broom fibres.
China pays up to 37.5% extra (25% List 3 + 12.5%); Brazil 37.5%; Canada 50% under Section 338 on six subheadings, even with a USMCA claim.
USMCA-qualifying plant material from Mexico — 49% of 2025 imports — enters free. The IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026 and the Section 122 surcharge expired July 23, 2026.
Entry rules matter more than duty for several lines: Lacey Act declarations, APHIS permits for broomcorn and cotton linters, and the hemp THC limit that tightens on December 11, 2026.

faqs.question: What are vegetable plaiting materials (HTS Chapter 14)?
faqs.answer: Raw plant materials used mainly for weaving and basketry — bamboo, rattan, reeds, rushes, willow (osier), raffia, cleaned or dyed cereal straw and lime bark — classified in heading 1401. Chapter 14 also holds heading 1404, vegetable products not elsewhere specified: cotton linters, vegetable hair, broomcorn, istle and other broom fibres, dyeing and tanning materials and a catch-all line. Textile fibres such as coir or hemp fibre are in section XI, and baskets made from plaiting materials are heading 4602.

faqs.question: What does HS code 1404.90 cover?
faqs.answer: Vegetable products not elsewhere specified other than cotton linters: 1404.90.10 vegetable hair (0.5¢/kg), 1404.90.20 broomcorn ($4.95/t), 1404.90.30 istle (Free), 1404.90.40 other broom and brush fibres (2.3%) and the Free basket line 1404.90.90 (dyeing and tanning materials and other products). 1404.90 was 91% of Chapter 14 imports in 2025 ($203M). All of 1404.90.90 is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for bamboo, and what is the tariff?
faqs.answer: Raw bamboo — whole, split, cut to length, polished or dyed, including poles and garden stakes — is 1401.10.00.00, Free at the general rate. Bamboo from China pays 37.5% (25% List 3 + 12.5%); from Indonesia, Cambodia, Ecuador, Malaysia, Taiwan, Bangladesh or Argentina it pays nothing extra (exception lists); from most other Section 301 economies 10% or 12.5%; from Canada 50%. Finished bamboo articles such as baskets are classified elsewhere (basketwork is heading 4602).

faqs.question: What Section 301 tariffs apply to raw bamboo and rattan from China?
searchedAs: china section 301 tariffs on raw bamboos
faqs.answer: Bamboo (1401.10.00), willow and other plaiting materials are on List 3 (+25%, 9903.88.03); rough rattan is on List 4A (+7.5%, 9903.88.15); split rattan (1401.20.40) is on no China list. The 2026 Section 301 action adds +12.5% (9903.05.31). Totals: bamboo 37.5%, willow 41.9%, rough rattan 20%, split rattan 14.5%. USTR confirmed on October 7, 2026 that the 2018 actions continue.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for rattan?
faqs.answer: Raw rattan is 1401.20: 1401.20.20 for rattan in the rough or cut transversely into sections (Free; .10 for pieces 4 meters or longer) and 1401.20.40 for other rattan, such as cores and split or drawn rattan (2%). Rattan furniture, baskets and bags are not Chapter 14 — they are chapter 94 or heading 4602. Indonesian, Cambodian, Ecuadorian and Jordanian raw rattan is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for coco peat and coir pith?
searchedAs: hs code for coco peat block
faqs.answer: CBP classifies coco peat (coir pith), coco peat blocks and coconut husk chips in 1404.90.90.90, Free (rulings N241191, N250256, N270127). Coir fibre itself is 5305 and coir mats or rope are other chapters. 1404.90.90 is on the Section 301 general exemption list, so coco peat from India and Sri Lanka enters free; from Canada it pays the 50% Section 338 duty.

faqs.question: Does the U.S. import coco peat, and from where?
faqs.answer: Yes, inside the 1404.90 catch-all. UN Comtrade does not split 1404.90 further, but India ($31M) and Sri Lanka ($9M) — the suppliers named in CBP's coco peat rulings — shipped almost all their Chapter 14 goods under heading 1404 in 2025, both up 52% from 2024. Imports need country-of-origin marking; any wood pallets must be ISPM 15 treated.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and import duty for cotton linters?
searchedAs: hs code for cotton linter pulp
faqs.answer: Cotton linters are 1404.20.00.00, Free at the general rate; cotton linters pulp is a separate product, 4706.10.00.00. Linters pay the country's Section 301 rate (10% India, 12.5% Türkiye), 37.5% from China and 50–60% from Canada. APHIS requires vacuum fumigation or movement to an approved mill unless the linters were processed so that no seed or insect life remains (7 CFR 319.8-7, 319.8-8). U.S. imports jumped from $0.8M to $3.5M in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for henna?
searchedAs: hs code for natural henna powder
faqs.answer: Dried henna leaves are 1404.90.90.40 (raw vegetable materials used primarily in dyeing), Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty (CBP ruling N262445). Prepared henna hair dyes and mixes can be classified elsewhere — CBP put one henna powder product in 3212.90 (ruling B85634) — so get a ruling for blended products. FDA approves henna as a color additive only for hair, not skin (21 CFR 73.2190).

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for raffia, willow and seagrass?
faqs.answer: Raw willow (osier) is 1401.90.20 at 4.4%, and other plaiting materials — raffia (CBP ruling N015584), reeds, rushes, straw — are 1401.90.40 at 3.2%. Baskets made from them are heading 4602 (willow baskets 4602.19.12 or .22). From the EU these raw materials pay 10% in total; from China 41.9% (willow) or 40.7%.

faqs.question: Can you import hemp flower, and what is its HS code?
faqs.answer: CBP classifies dried hemp flower and hemp biomass in 1404.90.90, Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty (HQ H334131, July 23, 2026). It is importable only if it meets the federal hemp definition: today not more than 0.3% delta-9 THC; from December 11, 2026 (P.L. 119-103) total THC including THCA. Above that it is marijuana, a controlled substance. Hemp fibre is 5302.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on Chapter 14 goods from Mexico?
searchedAs: mexico tariff on vegetable plaiting materials
faqs.answer: Not on goods that qualify for USMCA — plant material grown in Mexico is originating. USMCA goods pay no base rate and are exempt from Mexico's 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.94). Without a valid claim, the base rate plus 10% applies, except 1404.90.90 goods, which pay nothing extra either way. The 25% IEEPA duty ended February 24, 2026. Broomcorn also needs an APHIS permit. Mexico supplied $108M, 49% of Chapter 14 imports, in 2025.

faqs.question: Why do Canadian Chapter 14 goods pay 50%?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on imports from canada
faqs.answer: Since August 22, 2026 a 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14, Proclamation 11048) applies to Canadian bamboo, willow, other plaiting materials, cotton linters, other broom fibres and all of 1404.90.90, and U.S. note 51(a) charges it even when USMCA is claimed. Rattan, vegetable hair, broomcorn and istle are not on that list and enter free under USMCA. No Chapter 14 line is on the September 29, 2026 import bans.

faqs.question: How much does the U.S. import under HTS Chapter 14?
faqs.answer: $222M in 2025, up 10.4% from $201M in 2024. The 1404.90 catch-all was $203M (91%), bamboo $13M (down 22%), cotton linters $3.5M and rattan $1.9M. Mexico supplied 49%, India 14%, China 9% and Sri Lanka 4%.
